summary.title: Differential recursion and differentially algebraic functions
summary.executive_summary: This paper critically re-examines Moore's theory of real recursive functions, which were proposed as a model for analog computation analogous to Kleene's discrete recursion. The author identifies significant ambiguities in Moore's original definitions, particularly regarding the handling of partial functions and the differential recursion operator. By rigorously reformulating the class of real primitive recursive functions to ensure mathematical soundness—specifically by enforcing analyticity and strict domain definitions—the paper demonstrates that Moore's central claim (Claim 1) fails. The study proves that even under the most restrictive, well-defined formulation, real primitive recursive functions are not necessarily differentially algebraic. A specific counterexample involving the Euler gamma function is constructed, showing that a function can be real primitive recursive without being differentially algebraic. Consequently, the paper concludes that Moore's classes do not accurately model the General Purpose Analog Computer (GPAC) or Shannon's analog computation model, necessitating a search for new subclasses that might bridge the gap between digital recursion and analog differentiability.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper critically re-examines Moore's theory of real recursive functions, which were proposed as a model for analog computation analogous to Kleene's discrete recursion. The author identifies significant ambiguities in Moore's original definitions, particularly regarding the handling of partial functions and the differential recursion operator. By rigorously reformulating the class of real primitive recursive functions to ensure mathematical soundness—specifically by enforcing analyticity and strict domain definitions—the paper demonstrates that Moore's central claim (Claim 1) fails. The study proves that even under the most restrictive, well-defined formulation, real primitive recursive functions are not necessarily differentially algebraic. A specific counterexample involving the Euler gamma function is constructed, showing that a function can be real primitive recursive without being differentially algebraic. Consequently, the paper concludes that Moore's classes do not accurately model the General Purpose Analog Computer (GPAC) or Shannon's analog computation model, necessitating a search for new subclasses that might bridge the gap between digital recursion and analog differentiability.

Research Context
Theoretical models of real function computability include discrete approximation and continuous time models. Shannon's General Purpose Analog Computer models the Differential Analyzer and generates differentially algebraic functions. Moore introduced real recursive functions to express the power of GPAC-like computation. Moore claimed his real primitive recursive functions are differentially algebraic, linking them to analog computation. Moore's work lacked formality and contained technical inaccuracies regarding partial functions.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The paper investigates the validity of Moore's claims regarding the relationship between real recursive functions and analog computation. The central hypothesis is that Moore's original definitions are ambiguous and lead to erroneous claims about the class's properties. The study hypothesizes that a rigorous reformulation will reveal that real primitive recursive functions are not differentially algebraic. The paper aims to resolve the ambiguity of the differential recursion operator on partial functions. It is predicted that the purported relation to differentially algebraic functions fails under a sound mathematical formulation.

Methodological Details
The study focuses on the class of real primitive recursive functions defined by Moore. The analysis considers partial functions where the domain is a proper subset of the input space. A function is defined as analytic if it can be represented by a convergent power series on an open set. The domain of a composed function is the intersection of the domains of its components. The differential recursion operator requires a unique solution to an integral equation on the largest possible interval. The class is defined as the smallest class containing basic functions and closed under specific operators. Basic functions include constants, projections, addition, multiplication, and specific transcendental functions like exp and sin. The study relies on the Uniqueness Theorem for initial value problems to ensure analyticity.

Procedures And Architectures
The differential recursion operator dr is defined via an integral equation involving functions f and g. The operator dr(f, g) maps inputs to the unique solution hv defined on the largest interval. The class of real primitive recursive functions is the closure of basic functions under juxtaposition, composition, and dr. The study constructs specific functions like inv+ (1/x) and sqrt+ using integral equations. Trigonometric functions are constructed using a system of differential equations derived from integral definitions. The Euler gamma function is defined as a limit of a real primitive recursive function ˇΓ. The proof involves taking the limit of a polynomial relation satisfied by ˇΓ to derive a contradiction.

Key Results
Theorem 3 establishes the equivalence of various definitions of differentially algebraic functions. Theorem 8 proves that the property of being differentially algebraic is preserved by juxtaposition and composition. Theorem 12 states that if g is analytic, the solution set Hv consists of restrictions of a unique solution. Theorem 12 also states that if f and g are analytic, the resulting function dr(f, g) is analytic. The function ˇΓ is shown to be real primitive recursive using the established lemmas. The Euler gamma function Γ is known to be not differentially algebraic based on H¨older's result. The limit of the polynomial relation for ˇΓ yields a contradiction for Γ, disproving Claim 1. The study concludes that real primitive recursive functions are not necessarily differentially algebraic.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The failure of Claim 1 implies that Moore's classes do not model the General Purpose Analog Computer. The rigorous treatment of partial functions is essential to avoid ambiguous and erroneous statements. The analyticity of the differential recursion operator is crucial for maintaining the theoretical properties of the class. The study suggests that the relationship between digital recursion and analog computation is more complex than previously thought. The paper calls for finding a subclass of real primitive recursive functions that has a close relationship to differentially algebraic functions.

Contradictions And Limitations
Moore's original definition allows for inconsistencies regarding the domain of composed functions. The use of the relaxed operator drC leads to non-analytic functions, breaking the theoretical framework. The class of real recursive functions with minimization is probably not well-behaved due to non-smooth functions. The study does not know if the Euler gamma function Γ itself is real primitive recursive. The paper notes that Moore's real recursive functions can be discontinuous, unlike the analytic real primitive recursive functions.

Claims
Real primitive recursive functions are differentially algebraic. Moore claimed this relation in his original work. The definition of differentially algebraic functions is well-established. The Euler gamma function is not differentially algebraic. The limit of the polynomial relation for ˇΓ contradicts the claim for Γ. The study proves that even the most restrictive formulation fails. Moore's model does not accurately represent analog computation. New subclasses must be found to bridge the gap.
The differential recursion operator preserves analyticity under strict definitions. If f and g are analytic, so is the result of differential recursion. The solution to the integral equation is unique and analytic. Relaxing the definition to drC produces non-analytic functions. The function k derived via drC is not differentiable at 1. Strict definitions are necessary for theoretical consistency. Loose definitions lead to incomparable functions.

Data And Code Availability
The paper is a theoretical analysis and does not provide data or code.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study compares the standard operator dr with the relaxed operator drC. The analysis shows that drC fails to preserve analyticity.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the concept of a unique solution on the largest possible interval. Figure 2 shows an integrand with a singularity that affects the relaxed operator drC.

Three Takeaways
The paper rigorously disproves Moore's claim that real primitive recursive functions are differentially algebraic. The study highlights the critical importance of properly handling partial functions in analog computation theory. Future work must identify a subclass of real primitive recursive functions that relates closely to differentially algebraic functions.
